Everyone's Doing It
Somebody says a thing is right because everybody does it.
Lots of people can be wrong together. Ask for the real reason.
Only Two Doors
Somebody says you must pick this or that, and nothing else.
Look for a third door. There almost always is one.
The Tear Trick
Somebody uses sad or scary feelings to push you.
Feelings are real, but they are not reasons. Ask what is true.
The Lucky Socks
Somebody says one thing caused another only because it came first.
Coming first does not mean causing. Ask what else changed.
The Hot Streak
Somebody says a win must come soon because they lost many times.
Dice and cards do not remember. Every roll starts fresh.
Already Paid
Somebody says you must keep paying because you already paid a lot.
Money you spent is gone. Only ask if the next coin is worth it.
The Big Jump
Somebody meets one person and decides everybody like them is the same.
One person is not everyone. Judge each person by what they do.
The Insult Trick
Somebody attacks the person instead of answering what they said.
Who says something does not make it right or wrong. Look at the idea.
The Scarecrow
Somebody twists what you said into something silly, then knocks it down.
Ask yourself: is that really what I said?
Look Over There!
Somebody changes the subject so they do not have to answer.
Ask yourself: did they answer my question?
Big Hat Says
Somebody says a thing is true because an important person said it.
Important people need reasons too. Ask for the proof.
The Big Slide
Somebody says one small step will surely lead to something terrible.
Every step needs its own proof. One step is not a slide.
Always Done It
Somebody says the old way is best because it is the old way.
Old does not mean right. Ask if it still works.

You arrive in Riverside Village. You have 40 coins in your pouch.
A grey fog hangs over the valley. The fog grows every time a bad argument wins.
Use the arrows to walk. Press A to talk. People with a ! above their head want something from you.
Earn coins by doing jobs. Keep your coins away from tricksters. Then build something that helps everyone.
The gate swings open. You walk into River Farms.
People here love to say there are only two choices. There are almost always more.
The farmers need a way across the river. Find a carpenter and a surveyor, and bring your mason.
You cross your new bridge and walk into Market Town.
Two tricks live here. Some people push on your feelings. Others say "this came first, so it caused that."
The town wants an Engineering School. Experts learn faster when they train there.
The students cleared the rockfall. The road to the Hill Mine is open.
Hold on to your pouch. Gamblers here believe luck is "due". Sellers say you must keep paying because you already paid.
The miners need a waterwheel mill on the river to crush their ore.
The harbour wall opens. You smell salt and hear the gulls.
Every trick you have ever heard lives here, all at once.
Ships crash on the rocks every winter. Build a lighthouse, and the fog will lift from the whole Valley.
The Village Well
Your crew rolls up their sleeves. Work on the well begins!
The fog lifts from River Farms.
The village drinks muddy river water. A well in the square would give clean water. People will pay a coin to fill their buckets.
Clean water bubbles up from the ground. The whole village cheers.
Elder Otto opens the south gate. He says, "River Farms could use a builder like you."
The River Bridge
Your crew rolls up their sleeves. Work on the bridge begins!
The fog lifts from Market Town.
The ferry is the only way across, and the ferryman charges what he likes. A bridge would carry carts, and a small toll would pay you back.
The last plank drops into place. Carts roll across the river for the first time.
Ferryman Gus grumbles. Everyone else is delighted. Market Town lies ahead.
Engineering School
Your crew rolls up their sleeves. Work on the school begins!
The fog lifts from the Hill Mine.
Market Town has clever young people and nobody to teach them. A school earns fees, and your crew can train there to learn faster.
The school bell rings. Students run in with their notebooks.
The first class measures the rockfall north of town and clears a path to the Hill Mine.
The Waterwheel Mill
Your crew rolls up their sleeves. Work on the mill begins!
The fog lifts from the Harbour.
The miners crush ore by hand, and it takes forever. A waterwheel would do it a hundred times faster. The mine will pay well for it.
The wheel turns. The ore crunches. The miners whoop and throw their hats.
The foreman unlocks the harbour wall. She says, "Go on. The coast needs you more than we do."
The Lighthouse
Your crew rolls up their sleeves. Work on the lighthouse begins!
Ships crash on the rocks every winter. A lighthouse at the end of the pier would guide them home. It would also lift the fog from the whole Valley.
The great lamp flares. Its beam sweeps across the sea.
All over the Valley, the fog thins and then vanishes. Clear heads make clear skies.
Bread for the barn
Farmer Idris ordered six loaves, but I cannot leave my oven.
Please carry them to his barn in the south-east. He will pay you 12 coins.
Here you go. They are still warm. Mind the goats!
Idris waits by the barn in the south-east. Go down the lane and turn left.
You brought the bread! You saved my lunch. Here are 12 coins, as I promised.
Idris told me the bread was perfect. You run fast.
The lost goat
My goat Pickle ran off again. She likes the trees behind the barn.
Please bring her home. I will give you 10 coins.
She is white and she wears a bell. Listen for it.
Pickle likes the trees behind the barn, in the far south-east corner.
You find Pickle chewing a bush behind the barn.
You take her bell in your hand and lead her home.
You found Pickle! Here are 10 coins. You earned them.
Pickle has stayed home since you found her. Thank you.
The broken fence
The goats knocked down my fence on the west side of the field.
Please fix the rails. I will pay you 12 coins.
I left a hammer and nails by the gap. Mind your thumbs.
The gap is on the west side of my field, next to the square.
You line up the rails and hammer them straight.
The fence looks as good as new.
That fence is straighter than the one I built! Here are 12 coins.
The fence is holding. The goats are furious.
Apple harvest
The trees are dropping apples faster than I can pick them.
Please fill the basket in the orchard, to the north-west. I will pay you 30 coins.
The basket sits under the trees. Fill it right to the top.
The orchard is north-west of my farm. Follow the lane north.
You pick apples until the basket is heavy and your arms ache.
You count about two hundred apples.
You picked a proper harvest! Here are 30 coins, and take an apple for the road.
I am baking apple pie tonight. Come by if you like.
Seeds for Old Sal
Old Sal in the village wants bean seeds for the spring.
Please take this bag to her cottage. She will pay you 30 coins when it arrives.
Hold it tight. If you drop it, there will be beans everywhere.
Sal lives in the village, in the south-west, back through the gate.
You brought my bean seeds, just in time! Here are 30 coins. Please thank Pia for me.
I planted the beans already. You did good work.
The fallen scarecrow
Our scarecrow fell over, and now the crows are having a party.
Please stand him up again at the bottom of the big field. I will pay 30 coins.
His hat fell in the mud somewhere. Good luck.
The scarecrow lies at the bottom of the big field, east of the lane.
You heave the scarecrow up, straighten his hat, and tie his arms.
The crows fly away in a huff.
The crows are gone! Here are 30 coins, and thank you.
We have not seen a crow for a week.
Parcel to the Town Hall
This parcel is for Clerk Ossian at the Town Hall. I think it holds papers. Heavy ones.
Please deliver it. He will pay you 45 coins.
Be careful, the string is loose. The Town Hall stands north of the square.
The Town Hall stands at the top of the square. Ossian waits outside.
You brought the deeds! At last. Here are 45 coins. The town thanks you.
Ossian says the papers were the deeds for the school land. You came at the right time.
The dark lamp
The lamp in the south-west corner of the square has been dark for weeks.
Please climb up and light it again. The town will pay you 45 coins.
You will find matches in the base. Mind the ladder.
The dark lamp stands at the south-west corner of the square.
You climb up, clean the glass, and strike a match.
Warm light spills over the cobbles.
We have light at last! Here are 45 coins from the town purse.
The square feels much friendlier at night now.
The missing sign
Somebody stole my shop sign! I heard it is lying in the field north-east of the hall.
Please bring it back. I will pay you 45 coins.
It is a big wooden sign that says SHOP. You cannot miss it.
Look in the grass north-east of the Town Hall, near the trees.
You find the sign lying face-down in the grass. It is muddy but whole.
You lift it onto your shoulder and carry it back.
You found my sign! Here are 45 coins and my thanks.
Business is better now that people can find me.
Lamp oil for the mine
The miners are working in the dark. This can of lamp oil must reach Quill at the mine mouth.
Please carry it there. You will get 75 coins.
Do not spill it, and do not stand near the camp fire.
Quill waits at the mine entrance, north-east, up the road.
You brought the oil! Now we can see the ore we are hitting. Here are 75 coins, friend.
Quill says the lamps are burning bright.
The broken ore cart
Our ore cart lost a wheel on the road south of here.
Please fix it. The mine will pay you 75 coins.
We strapped a spare wheel underneath. It is heavy, mind.
The cart sits on the grass south of the mine, near the road.
You lift the cart onto a rock and bolt the wheel back on.
You give it a push. It rolls.
The cart is rolling again! Here are 75 coins from the mine.
That cart has hauled ten loads since you fixed it.
The escaped canary
Our canary flew out of her cage! She keeps the miners safe from bad air.
She likes the bushes north-east of the mine. Please bring her back. I will pay 75 coins.
Whistle to her. She likes whistling.
Look in the grass north-east of the mine, up by the rocks.
You whistle. A yellow flash lands on your shoulder.
She sings all the way back.
You found Goldie! She is safe and sound. Here are 75 coins.
Goldie is singing again, and the miners are happy.
The lost oar
The tide took my best oar. It washed up on the west beach, past the old footbridge.
Please bring it back. I will pay you 90 coins.
It is long, and the handle is carved. My father made it.
Cross the old footbridge to the west, then walk along the beach.
You spot a long oar with a carved handle, half buried in the sand.
You dig it out and shake off the seaweed.
You found my father's oar! Here are 90 coins. You have no idea what this means to me.
Orla rows out every morning now.
Fish for the tavern
This crate of fish must reach Bea at the Tavern before it goes off.
She pays 90 coins for a fresh crate.
Go quickly. If you get lost, follow your nose.
Walk west along the quay, then go up. Bea stands outside the Tavern.
This fish is as fresh as the sea! Here are 90 coins, and I will give you a bowl of chowder if you want one.
Bea says that was the best crate all season.
The tavern ledger
Lin forgot her ledger here. Without it she cannot sell a single fish.
Please take it back to her on the quay. I will pay you 90 coins.
It is the blue book. Do not get it wet.
Lin stands on the quay next to the pier.
You brought my ledger! I would have lost a whole day. Here are 90 coins.
Lin keeps the ledger on a string now.
Carry water
Fill the two buckets at the river.
Carry the water to Baker Hana at the bakery.
Thank you for the water! Here are 4 coins.
Milk the goats
Milk the goats in the pen.
Carry the pail of milk to Rin.
Fresh milk! Here are 5 coins.
Sweep the square
Sweep the square with the broom.
Sort ore
Sort the shiny ore out of the rock pile.
Carry the basket of ore to Cook Mab.
Good ore! Here are 8 coins.
Coil ropes
Coil the wet ropes on the quay.
Nothing more to do here yet. Come back in a little while.
Your hands are full. Deliver what you are carrying first.
Your crew learned a lot from the work. Open the Crew panel to see how much.
We ARE working. Look, it is going up right now.
We finished it. Tell me when the next job opens.
This job does not need my craft. Call me when something does.
I am not skilled enough for this job yet.
More building will teach me. So would a lesson at the school.
I cannot build it alone. We still need more experts.
Look at the site to see who is missing. Find them and clear their heads.
We are ready. We only need more coins.
Look at the top of the screen to see how many. Then press A at the site.
Everything is ready! Go to the site and press A. I will be right behind you.
A goat. It looks at you. You look at it.
A basket of apples under the trees.
A scarecrow, face down in the mud.
A fence rail hangs loose.
A street lamp.
A wooden sign lying in the grass.
An ore cart with a missing wheel.
A small yellow bird, singing.
An oar, half buried in sand.
Two buckets by the river.
A broom leaning on a stall.
A heap of rock with glints of ore.
Coils of wet rope.
The goats need milking.
A boat. It bobs.
A market stall. Bright things, high prices.
Cool water splashes.
A card table. The cards look tired.
A signpost.
A bench. Nobody is sitting.
Freshly cut timber.
A surveyor's tripod.
A crate. Heavy.
A flower pot.
The bridge toll box.
Nothing to do here.
Elder Otto
Welcome to Riverside, {name}. The fog comes from tricky talk. Clear heads clear it away.
The village needs a well. We marked the spot in the square. It costs coins, and it needs a water engineer and a mason.
Wren camps by the river. Mo the mason sits by the north lane. Both of them are a bit foggy in the head.
Baker Hana
I bake fresh bread every morning. If you want steady coins, carry water from the river for me. The buckets sit by the bank.
Farmer Idris
The goats break something every single day.
Old Sal
My knees know when rain is coming. Today they say no rain.
Mo the Mason
Why you stayed behind
You want me to work? No. All the other masons left for the city.
Everyone says there is no work in this valley. If everyone left, they must be right.
So I sit here. Why should I be the only mason who stays?
Everyone leaving doesn't prove there's no work. There's a well to build.
You're right. If every other mason left, the work must really be gone from here.
The other masons were cowards. Don't be a coward.
A well? Here? Huh.
Everyone said there was no work, and I never looked for myself.
Fine. Show me the site. I charge 10 coins a job.
That is what I said. So we agree. There is no work.
Mo goes back to staring at the river.
River sand for the mortar
Everyone in the village mixes their mortar with river sand. Everyone does it, so it must be the best way.
I will use river sand on your well.
Everyone using it doesn't make it best. Let's test a brick first.
Everyone does it and nobody complains, so yes, river sand will be fine for the well.
Everyone in this village is a fool.
You want to test it? Fine. Look, the river sand crumbles. The pit sand holds.
Everyone was wrong together. My head feels lighter already.
Right. I will use river sand.
A month later, the mortar crumbles. Everyone was wrong together.
I am ready when you are. Stone does not build itself.
Wren
Wells in this valley
You want a well? Nobody digs wells around here. Nobody ever has.
If wells worked, everybody would have one. Nobody does. So wells do not work here.
I dig ditches. Everyone wants ditches.
Nobody trying doesn't prove it won't work. Let's test the ground.
Fair point. If nobody in the whole valley has one, wells must not work here.
Ditch-diggers don't know anything about wells.
You want to test the ground? I have a probe rod. Give me a moment.
I found water. It sits four metres down. Nobody ever checked.
All right, builder. I charge 15 coins a job, and I am yours.
Exactly. Now, let us talk about ditches.
Wren goes back to sharpening her spade.
Digging at the full moon
Everyone says you must dig a well at the full moon, or it runs dry.
I know it sounds odd, but everyone says it. So we wait two weeks.
Everyone saying it isn't evidence. Water doesn't care about the moon.
If everyone says it, there must be something in it. Let's wait for the full moon.
Everyone in this valley is superstitious and silly.
The moon does not reach four metres underground, does it?
I feel clearer now. I learn faster with a clear head.
We wait. Two weeks pass and nothing happens.
The well works exactly the same as it would have. Everyone was wrong together.
Water always finds a way. So do we.
Pip
It turns out the pebbles are just pebbles. Do you want one for free?
Dodge
Fine, fine. The cups game is a trick. Please don't tell the others.
Farmer Pia
A bridge would double my sales. Half my apples rot while they wait for the ferry.
Ren
My sister and I argue about the field every single spring.
Rin
We should plant beans. Or wheat. It has to be one or the other!
We plant half and half now. Why did that take us five years?
Ferryman Gus
A bridge, eh? I suppose I could sell boat rides for fun instead.
Lotto Lou
You can be a winner, a quitter, or a person who keeps their coins. Fine, you win.
Cass
Working for the sawmill boss
You want to hire a carpenter? Not me.
Either I work for the sawmill boss for pennies, or I do not work at all. Those are my two choices.
I chose "not at all".
Those aren't the only two. Work for me, on a bridge, for a fair fee.
That's a hard choice, and I understand picking neither. Better idle than underpaid.
The sawmill boss is a crook, so you should hate him.
You want me to work for you? On a bridge?
I never thought of a third door. I was too busy hating door number one.
I charge 25 coins a job. We have a deal.
You see? Even you agree. There are two doors, and both are bad.
Cass goes back to whittling a stick.
Oak or pine for the deck
We must pick wood for the bridge deck. Either we use oak and it takes a year, or we use pine and it rots in two winters.
Pick one. Slow or rotten.
Or pine deck we can replace, on oak beams that last.
Oak then. A year is fine, this bridge should last a hundred.
Pine. Rotting is fine, we'll worry about that in two winters.
Oak bones and pine skin. Ha! Yes!
I saw two doors, and there was a window the whole time.
If you say so.
The bridge could have been better. There was a third way.
I measure twice, I cut once, and I never argue.
Sy
Measuring the river
You want me to measure the river for a bridge? That is impossible.
Either the King's surveyors measure it with their brass tools, or nobody measures it at all.
And the King's men never come here.
You have a tripod and a rope. Measure it yourself.
True. Without the King's men and their brass tools, nothing here can be measured properly.
The King's men are lazy snobs anyway.
You want me to do it myself? With my own tripod?
The river is twenty-two paces wide, bank to bank. I just measured it.
I charge 20 coins a job, and I am on your crew.
Exactly. So we wait for the King. We will wait forever.
Sy polishes his glasses and stares at the water.
Where the bridge should go
The bridge must go right here at the ferry, or it must not go anywhere.
If we put it anywhere else, the whole plan fails.
Or upstream where the banks are rock. More than two places exist.
Here or nowhere, and the farms need a crossing. Here, then, on the mud.
Nowhere. Forget the bridge.
The rock banks! Of course. I only ever looked at two spots.
My head feels clearer. I can see more doors now.
We build it here, on the soft mud.
The bridge could have been better. Two choices were never the only choices.
I like straight lines and honest numbers.
Vell
All right, the puppy is fine. He is fat, actually. You are a hard one to fool.
Zia
Maybe the new stall spot did it, and not the charm. Hmm.
Fortune Mags
You see too clearly for my trade. Go and build your school.
Auctioneer Bram
A fair price is a fair price. Even I know that on a good day.
Innkeeper Dot
We have rooms upstairs and soup downstairs.
Clerk Ossian
I fill in forms all day. The school will need a licence. I have already stamped it.
Shopkeeper Nell
I sell rope, nails and lamp oil. If I sell it, you need it.
Professor Ada
The students who cried
You want me to teach at a school? Never again.
Last year two students failed their exam and cried in my library. I cannot bear that again.
How can a school be a good idea when it makes children cry?
Tears are real, but not a reason. Did the students who passed learn?
You're right, anything that makes children cry is a bad idea, however useful.
Crying students are weak. Ignore them.
Did they learn? Forty of them passed. Two of them cried.
I let two tears decide for forty students.
Very well. I charge 40 coins a job, and I will run your school.
Then we agree. There will be no school.
Ada returns to her book.
The lucky green scarf
I always lecture in my green scarf. The one year I forgot it, three students failed.
The scarf must be lucky. I cannot teach without it, and it is at the cleaners.
The scarf came first. Did it cause the passes? What else changed?
Then we wait for the scarf, it's not worth risking a whole year of students.
Scarves are silly. Throw it away.
What else changed? I was ill that year, and I missed six lectures.
The scarf never mattered. My head feels clearer already.
We wait for the scarf.
Coming first was never the same as causing.
Knowledge is the only building that grows when you share it.
Brick
The bell tower that fell
I laid the last stones on the bell tower. A week later, it fell down.
My stones caused it. My hands are cursed. I will never lay stone again.
Your stones came before the fall. Was the ground checked?
If it fell a week after your stones, your stones did it. Best leave building to others.
Curses aren't real, you superstitious oaf.
The ground? The surveyor said the ground was soft. Nobody listened to him.
My hands are fine. The ground did it.
I charge 35 coins a job. Let me build something that stands.
I am cursed. I told you.
Brick stares at his hands.
I keep it level, plumb and square. Every time.
Ace
So cards have no memory, eh? You would make a terrible customer.
Sterling
The Dry Gulch shaft is dry. There, I said it.
Grit
One man from Dale cheated me. One. And I blamed the whole town for it.
Foreman Tam
A mill would change everything up here. Fen knows how to build one. Fen just needs a clear head.
Quill
It is dark down there. Very dark.
Cook Mab
I cook stew for the miners. If you want coins, sort the ore at the pile east of here.
Fen
Three fallen mills
You want me to build a mill? Oh, I will. But I will not use a plan.
My last three mills fell down. Three failures in a row! So this one is due to work.
Luck has to turn. I do not need drawings. Let us just start.
Three failures don't make a success due. Why did they fall?
Three in a row! You're definitely due. Let's start now before the luck wears off.
Three failures? You are obviously a terrible millwright.
Why did they fall? The wheel was too heavy for the axle. It happened all three times.
Luck was never coming. A stronger axle is.
I charge 60 coins a job, and I will draw it properly this time.
That is the spirit! We need no plan!
Fen picks up a hammer and a hopeful look.
The 400-coin design
I have spent 400 coins on a mill design that cannot work. The axle is wrong.
But I spent 400 coins! I cannot throw that away. I must spend 200 more to finish it.
The 400 is gone either way. Is the next 200 worth it? No.
You've spent so much already, you have to finish it or it was all for nothing.
You wasted 400 coins? Fool.
The next 200 coins would buy me a mill that falls down.
The 400 is gone whatever I do. That hurts. But I see it clearly now.
Right. I will spend 200 more.
Six hundred coins of mill fall into the river.
I draw a good wheel twice before I build it once.
Harbour Master Coyle
I checked. The Guild Master has never seen a storm from a boat.
Sailor Bo
I take one step at a time now. Lighthouses don't summon pirates. I knew that, really.
Merchant Vance
I may have twisted your words a little. It is a habit in my trade.
Captain Hale
We lit bonfires for two hundred years. And ships wrecked for two hundred years. Aye.
Dockhand Rook
Fine, the smith knows her metal. Even if she does have a funny accent.
Orla
The sea gives and the sea takes. Mostly it takes.
Fisher Lin
Rope work pays if you need coins. The coils sit further down the quay.
Cook Bea
I make chowder. I always make chowder.
Iva the Smith
What the Guild Master said
You want me to forge the great lamp for a lighthouse? No.
The Guild Master himself says a lamp that bright will crack in the sea wind.
He is the Guild Master. He wears the gold chain. He must be right.
A gold chain isn't a reason. Has any bright lamp cracked?
The Guild Master would know better than us. Best not risk it, the sea wind is fierce.
The Guild Master is an old fool.
Has any lamp cracked? He has never built a lamp. He only inspects ledgers.
I have built a hundred lamps. Not one of them cracked.
I charge 80 coins a job. Let me forge the biggest lamp yet.
Yes. Best not.
Iva bangs a horseshoe flat and thinks about gold chains.
One lamp leads to ruin
If I forge one giant lamp, every harbour will want one. Then I will never sleep. Then the forge will burn out. Then I will lose everything.
One lamp leads to ruin. So I will make no lamp.
One lamp doesn't force the next. You can say no later.
True, one lamp really could ruin you in the end. Better not start down that road.
You are just lazy.
I can say no to the second lamp. Ha! I can.
One step is not a slide. My head is as clear as a bell.
Then I will make no lamp. It is safer.
The slide was never real. One step is only one step.
Iron listens if you speak to it firmly.
I want to ask you one more thing, {name}. Some villagers say, "Nobody here has ever built a well, so nobody should."
They said it to me last night. Everyone was nodding. What do you make of that?
Everyone nodding isn't a reason. Has anyone checked?
If nobody has ever built one here, they probably know something we don't about the ground.
Those villagers sound stupid, and stupid people should not get a vote on this.
Ha! That is exactly what I hoped you would say.
Nobody has checked. So we should check. Take these 8 coins for the well fund. That is my share.
Hmm. That is what they said too. But is everyone agreeing a reason?
Otto looks disappointed. The fog around the square grows a little thicker.
Calling them names does not answer them, child.
Psst! {name}! I sell lucky pebbles. They cost ten coins.
Everyone in the village bought one. Hana bought one. Idris bought one. The twins bought one. Everyone!
You don't want to be the only one without a lucky pebble, do you?
Everyone has one? Then I'd better have one too. Here's 10 coins, I don't want to be the odd one out.
Everyone buying one doesn't make it lucky. What does it actually do?
You are a little cheat, Pip, and everybody in this village knows it.
You hand over 10 coins. Pip hands you a grey pebble.
It is a pebble. Later, Idris tells you he never bought one. Hana did not buy one either.
You paid ten coins for a pebble. "Everyone" turned out to be nobody.
It... um. It sits there. It sits there luckily.
OK, nobody bought one. You were my first try. Take 6 coins for not falling for it. I'm being honest, see?
I am not!
Pip runs off. You still do not know what the pebble does.
I have three cups and one pea. You pay fifteen coins to play. You win thirty if you find the pea!
Everybody plays this game. All the kids played today. Everybody loves it. Come on, join everybody!
Everybody plays and everybody loves it, so it must be fair. Fine, 15 coins, shuffle them.
Everybody playing doesn't mean anybody wins. How many won today?
Cheaters like you should be run out of town on the back of a cart.
You pay 15 coins. Dodge shuffles the cups so fast that they blur.
You pick the middle cup. It is empty. The pea was never under any of them.
Everybody played. Nobody won. A crowd doing something does not make it a good idea.
How many won? Er. About... none.
You're sharper than the others. Take 6 coins, and please don't tell Elder Otto.
Oi!
Dodge packs up his cups. A crowd gathers to argue about who is a cheat. Nobody asks how many people won.
Do you want to see the other side of the river? It is simple.
Either you pay me 30 coins for the ferry, or you never see the other side. Ever.
You have two choices. That is all there is.
If those are the only two choices, I suppose I have to pay. Here's 30 coins for the ferry.
Those aren't the only two. I could build a bridge.
You greedy old goat, no wonder nobody likes you.
You pay 30 coins. Gus rows you out, turns around halfway, and rows you back.
The trip across costs extra. You should have asked.
You paid thirty coins, and you are still on this side. Two doors were never the only doors.
A... bridge.
Nobody ever says that. Here, take 15 coins. Call it a gift for my retirement.
You are the goat!
You both stand on the bank and glare at each other. The river does not care.
I sell lotto tickets for 12 coins! The grand prize is 500!
Listen. In this life you are either a winner or a quitter.
Winners buy tickets. So which one are you?
I'm no quitter, and 500 coins would fix everything. Give me a ticket, here's 12.
Or a third option: someone who keeps their 12 coins.
Only losers sell lottery tickets, and only bigger losers buy them.
You buy a ticket. Lou draws a number. It is not yours.
You were so close! Winners try again.
Twelve coins are gone. "Winner or quitter" hid the real third door: keep your money.
A person who keeps their coins. That option is not on my sign.
To be honest, nobody has won yet. Take 15 coins for seeing the third door.
That is rude!
Lou sells three tickets to the people who came to watch the argument.
{name}! Please settle this for us. We should plant the big field with wheat. All wheat!
No! All beans! It is beans or wheat, one or the other, and Ren is wrong.
Well? Wheat or beans? Pick one!
You have to pick one, so wheat. It sells better and everyone around here grows it.
Why only one? Half wheat, half beans.
You two are the silliest farmers in the valley and I'm not surprised the crows visit.
Wheat?! Fine. We plant wheat.
The wheat catches a disease. The whole field is lost. Beans would have been fine in half of it.
Half... and half.
We argued for five years. Five years!
Take 15 coins. You ended a war.
Well, at least we agree that you are rude.
Please. Please. My puppy is starving. Look at my face. Look at it!
If you do not give me 20 coins right now, he will not eat tonight, and it will be your fault.
Do you want a puppy to starve? Do you?
No! Don't let him starve, that would be awful. Here, take 20 coins and buy him something.
Sorry you're upset, but feelings aren't reasons. Where's the puppy? Let's feed him.
Beggars are all liars.
You hand over 20 coins. Vell nods sadly and walks into the Inn.
Through the window, you see him order a pie. There is no puppy.
You paid twenty coins for a sad face. Feelings are real, but they are not reasons.
You want to feed him? He is, er, at my cousin's house. In another town.
Oh, all right. There is no puppy. You have a cool head. Take 15 coins, and I'll try honest work.
How dare you!
Now everyone is shouting. Nobody asks where the puppy is.
I sell prosperity charms! They cost 25 coins, and I guarantee them!
The day I hung this charm on my stall, my sales doubled. They doubled on the very same day!
The charm caused it. Obviously. Buy one and double your coins.
Sales doubled the very same day? That's proof enough for me. Sold, 25 coins.
It came first, but did it cause it? What else changed that day?
Charms are for idiots and people who believe in them deserve to lose their coins.
You buy the charm and hang it on your pouch.
Your coins do not double. You have 25 fewer.
The charm came first. Market day caused the sales. Coming first is not the same as causing.
What else changed? Well, that was the day I moved my stall next to the fountain.
Oh. Oh! The spot did it. Take 15 coins. You just saved me from buying twenty more charms.
Excuse me?!
I will tell your fortune for 15 coins, dear. And listen, it works.
Last week I told a farmer he would find gold. The next day he found a gold coin in his field!
I said it, and then it happened. My words made it happen. Pay 15 coins and hear yours.
You said it and then it happened, that can't be a coincidence. 15 coins, tell me mine.
Saying it first isn't causing it. Coins get lost in fields all the time.
Fortune tellers are all frauds.
You pay 15 coins. Mags peers at your palm.
You will spend money today. Ah! It has already come true!
You paid fifteen coins. She said it first, but saying a thing is not causing it.
Coins get lost in fields all the time. Yes. They do.
You have a clear eye, dear. Take 15 coins, and do not tell my customers.
Frauds? I see a rude future for you.
Going once! I am selling this fine vase. It is only slightly cracked. It can be yours for 30 coins, friend!
My poor old mother painted it. She would weep to see it unsold. She would weep!
You would not break an old woman's heart over 30 coins, would you?
I couldn't break an old woman's heart over a few coins. Fine, 30 coins for the vase.
Her feelings aren't a reason. Is a cracked vase worth 30? No.
Your mother probably cannot paint, and neither can you sell.
You pay 30 coins. The vase leaks.
My mother? Oh, she is fine. She never painted a thing in her life. Sold!
You paid thirty coins for a cracked vase and a made-up heartbreak.
Is it worth 30? No, it is not, is it. It is worth about 3.
You judge fairly! Take 15 coins. The market needs more heads like yours.
Leave my mother out of this!
Pick red or black, friend. You bet 40 coins, and you win double if you guess right.
And listen to this. Red has come up five times in a row. Five!
Black is due. It is overdue! Bet on black and you cannot lose.
Five reds in a row? Black is definitely due now. 40 coins on black, turn it over.
Cards don't remember. Five reds don't make black more likely.
You are a filthy card cheat and everyone at this table knows it.
You put 40 coins on black. Ace turns the card over.
It is red. That makes six in a row. Ace shrugs.
Wow. Now black is really due. Do you want to bet another 40?
Cards don't remember. Well. You've spoiled my game.
Take 20 coins for being honest. Most folk never work that out.
A cheat? Prove it.
You cannot prove it. Nobody talks about whether black was really "due".
I sell shares in the Dry Gulch shaft for just 20 coins! I guarantee there is silver down there.
What do you say? You pay a small stake for a big future.
All right, a small stake for a big future. 20 coins for a share.
No thanks. Show me the silver first.
Share sellers are all crooks.
You pay 20 coins. Sterling hands you a certificate.
Hmm, I have bad news. The shaft needs a new pump. Every shareholder must put in 30 more coins.
You have already put in 20. You cannot throw that away! Pay 30 more, or you lose it all.
I've already paid 20. If I stop now it's wasted. Here's 30 more, fix the pump.
The 20 is gone either way. Is the NEXT 30 worth it? No.
You planned this, you snake.
You pay 30 more coins.
Splendid. Oh dear, the pump broke. Can you spare another 40?
You dropped fifty coins into a dry hole. Money you already spent is gone. It never buys the next coin back.
The 20 is gone either way. Yes. Yes, it is.
Most people pay the 30. Then they pay the 40. Take your 20 back, and 20 more for the lesson.
You want to see the silver? Ah. The silver is, um, still in the ground.
You are a careful investor. That is rare. Take 20 coins. Call it a dividend.
Crooks! Nobody has ever insulted me so badly before lunch.
Do you need tools? Buy them from me. Never buy from Dale, up the hill.
A fellow from Dale sold me a cracked pick once. One fellow. So all Dale folk are cheats.
My picks cost 35 coins. Theirs cost 15. But theirs are Dale picks.
If a Dale man cheated you, the rest can't be trusted either. 35 coins for yours, then.
One cheat doesn't make all of Dale cheats. I'll judge each pick by itself.
You are the cheat here, old man.
You pay 35 coins for a pick that looks exactly like the 15-coin one.
You wasted twenty coins. One person from a place is not everyone from that place.
Judge each pick by itself. Hm. That is fair.
I blamed a whole town for one fellow. Take 20 coins, and buy a good pick wherever it comes from.
Old man?! I am barely seventy!
So you want a lighthouse? The Guild Master says bright lights attract storms.
He is the Guild Master. He wears the gold chain. So it must be true.
Luckily, I sell storm-charms. Pay 40 coins and your lighthouse will be safe.
If the Guild Master says so, who am I to argue? 40 coins for a storm-charm, to be safe.
A title isn't evidence. What's his proof that light attracts storms?
The Guild Master is a pompous fool.
You buy a storm-charm. It is a shell on a string.
Storms arrive exactly as often as before. Important people need reasons too.
His proof? He... said it at a dinner.
You ask hard questions. Take 25 coins and build your light. I will not tell the Guild.
I shall report that remark.
You want to build a lighthouse? Are you mad?
If you build a lighthouse, more ships will come. More ships will bring pirates. Pirates will burn the town. The town will be ash. Ash!
Unless you buy my pirate insurance. It costs 30 coins.
I don't want the town to burn, and that does sound like how it goes. 30 coins for insurance.
Each step needs its own proof. A light doesn't make pirates appear.
You are a coward, Bo.
You buy pirate insurance. It is a napkin with "INSURANCE" written on it.
No pirates come. You spent thirty coins on a slide that was never real.
Each step needs its own proof. I did run the steps together, didn't I?
Take 25 coins. Nobody ever stops me at step two.
A coward?! I have sailed through three gales!
You want a lighthouse at the end of the pier, yes?
Yes. I want to stop the wrecks.
So you are saying that every ship must be forced to dock here and pay you. You want a toll on the whole sea!
That is outrageous. Luckily, I sell "free sea" permits. Pay 35 coins and I will tell nobody about your sea-toll.
I don't want people thinking I'd tax the sea. 35 coins for the permit, and please keep quiet.
That's not what I said. A light to stop wrecks. Nothing about tolls.
You lying weasel merchant.
You buy a permit for a plan you never had.
You paid thirty-five coins to defend a scarecrow. Nobody said "sea toll" except Vance.
That is not what you said. No. It is not.
It is an old habit. I twist your words, and then I sell you the untwisting. Take 25 coins. You are hard to twist.
A weasel? I am a merchant!
A lighthouse? Bah. We have lit bonfires on the cliff for two hundred years.
Two hundred years! That is how we do it, so that is the best way to do it.
Give 45 coins to the bonfire fund instead, like every captain before you did.
Two hundred years of captains can't all be wrong. 45 coins for the bonfires, as always.
Old isn't the same as right. How many ships wrecked with the fires lit?
Old sailors are too stubborn to think.
You give 45 coins. The bonfire blows out in the first wind, just as it has for two hundred years.
They always did it this way. Ships always wrecked.
How many wrecked? Still plenty. Aye. Twelve wrecked last winter.
Two hundred years, and I never counted. Take 25 coins for the lamp. Make it bright.
Stubborn? I will show you stubborn.
You want Iva the Smith to forge your lamp? Her?
She talks funny. She comes from up the coast. She is short. You cannot trust a lamp from someone like that.
Buy a lamp from my cousin instead. Pay 30 coins as a deposit, today only.
If she's not the trustworthy type, I'd rather not risk it. 30 coins for your cousin's lamp.
Where she's from says nothing about her lamps. Has any Iva lamp failed?
You are the untrustworthy one, ugly.
You pay 30 coins. The cousin does not exist.
You lost thirty coins because someone insulted a smith. Who says a thing does not make it right or wrong.
Has any of her lamps failed? No. Not one.
I was just being nasty. Take 25 coins, and get your lamp from Iva.
Ugly?!
Now two people are insulting each other. Nobody talks about lamps.
Orla, the harbour fund is short by 50 coins. The ledger says you took them out.
The fund? Oh, look at that sunset! Have you ever seen colours like that? And look at the gulls!
You know what, let me tell you about the time a gull stole my hat.
That IS a lovely sunset. Go on then, tell me about the gull and your hat.
The sunset can wait. Orla, did you take the 50 coins?
Thief! You are a thief and everybody on this quay should know it!
The gull story lasts twenty minutes. The sun sets. The fund is still short.
Your question never got an answer. That was the whole point of the sunset.
Yes. I took them to fix my boat. I was going to put them back.
Here are 25 of them now. I will pay the rest next week. Thank you for not letting me wriggle away.
A thief?! After all I have done for this quay?
Now you are arguing about her character. Your question is still unanswered.
the Grey Order
A preacher of the Grey Order has left the lodge. Watch the map.
The preacher looks through you and says nothing.
The preacher stops at the edge of the circle and turns away.
The preacher leaves. A grey fog settles over a cleared head.
The preacher leaves. Someone will not work with you any more.
Statue of Aristotle
Aristotle wrote down the tricks of bad arguments long ago. Nobody inside the circle of his statue can be fooled by a preacher.
"It is the mark of an educated mind to entertain a thought without accepting it."
Needs a mason in your crew.
Your mason sets the plinth. The statue goes up.
The statue stands. Clear heads gather around it.
A stone plinth with nothing on it. Somebody should build a statue here.
Aristotle looks down at you from his plinth. Nobody inside his circle can be fooled by a preacher.
What the preacher knows
A preacher in grey came by. He has read more books than anyone in this valley.
He says stone that is cut on a Tuesday cracks in the frost. He knows many things, so he knows this too.
I will not cut stone this week. Ask me again next week.
Reading many books is not proof about stone. Has any Tuesday stone cracked?
He does sound very learned, and frost really does crack stone, so waiting a week is the careful choice.
Everyone respects the preacher, so we should respect what he says about stone too.
A week is nothing. Let the stone rest, and let the preacher have his little rule.
Has any cracked? I have cut stone on every day of the week for thirty years.
Knowing many things is not the same as knowing this thing. My head is clear again.
Next week, then.
Next week the preacher has a new rule. The work waits.
One crack leads to ruin
The preacher showed me a crack in an old wall. He was very calm about it.
He said one crack lets in water. Water makes two cracks. Two make ten. Ten bring the wall down, and then the whole village.
It made sense, step by step. So I will not build walls any more. Walls only fall.
Each step needs its own proof. Does one crack really make two?
He is right that water gets into cracks, so the safest thing is to build nothing that can crack.
That wall is old and badly built. Yours will be better, so it will never crack at all.
The preacher has never laid a stone in his life, so nothing he says about walls counts.
Does one crack make two? Only if nobody fills it. I fill cracks. That is my job.
He ran the steps together, and I ran after him. Not any more.
Yes. Nothing that can crack. So, nothing.
Mo sits on a pile of stone he will not use.
The dry spring
The preacher walked past the spring on the hill on Monday. On Tuesday the spring ran dry.
He says the ground is angry with us because we dig where we should not. He said it, and then the spring dried up.
If I dig for you again, the river might dry up next. I cannot risk that.
Walking past came first. Did it cause the drying? What else happened?
That is a strange thing to happen the very next day, so it is wise to stop digging until we understand it.
Springs dry up in summer all the time, and this one dried up because it is old, not because of any preacher.
The preacher is only trying to scare you, and people who scare others should not be listened to.
What else happened? It has not rained for three weeks. That is what happened.
The spring dried because the sky was dry. Coming first is not causing. I forgot that for a moment.
You are right. I will stop digging.
The spring comes back with the rain, and nobody says sorry.
The preacher's two paths
The preacher says every well is a choice. Either we trust the old river, as our grandparents did, or we trust holes in the ground and lose the river.
He put it so simply. River or hole. I cannot choose against the river.
Why only two? A well and the river can both give water.
When you put it like that, the river has kept us alive for years, so the river must come first.
Our grandparents drank from the river and they were fine, so the old way is clearly the right way.
The preacher wants us to stay thirsty so we stay weak, and a man like that should not choose for us.
Both? The well for drinking and the river for the fields.
He built two doors and hid the third. I nearly walked through his door.
The river, then. Only the river.
The village drinks muddy water for another year.
Bridges are not our way
The preacher in grey sat with me for an hour. He knows the old stories of this valley.
For three hundred years, he said, the farms used the ferry. Three hundred years cannot be wrong.
Who am I to cut a plank against three hundred years?
Old is not the same as right. Did the ferry serve the farms well?
Three hundred years is a long time, and a way that lasts that long has probably earned some respect.
Half the farmers want a bridge, so the old way has already lost, whatever the preacher says.
The ferry is Gus's business, and the preacher is probably a friend of Gus, so of course he wants the ferry.
Did it serve them well? Pia loses half her apples every year waiting for the ferry.
Three hundred years of rotten apples. Old is not the same as right.
I will not cut against the years.
Cass puts her saw away.
What the builder really wants
The preacher told me what you really want. You want to pave the whole river and drive the fish away.
I never said that. I want one bridge.
He explained it, though. One bridge, then two, then a road on the water. He was very sure. I cannot help someone who hates fish.
That is not what I said. One bridge. Nothing about paving a river.
I would never pave the river, I promise, and I like fish very much, so please help me anyway.
Even if there were a road on the water one day, more roads bring more trade, so it would not be so bad.
The preacher is a liar, and liars should be run out of the valley before they say anything else.
Nothing about paving? He said it as if you had said it.
He built a scarecrow of you and knocked it down. I clapped. I am sorry.
Hmm. That is what he said you would say.
Cass goes back to whittling. The river stays uncrossed.
The preacher's map
The preacher showed me a map. It has a gold seal from the capital.
On the map the river is forty paces wide. I measured twenty-two. But my rope is only a rope, and his map has a seal.
I must have measured wrong. I cannot plan anything on a wrong number.
A seal is not a measurement. Measure it again and trust the rope.
A map from the capital was made by trained people with proper tools, so forty paces is the safer number.
Twenty-two, forty, it hardly matters, just build everything long enough for both and be done with it.
Preachers do not know maps, and a man who cannot measure should not tell a surveyor his business.
Again? Twenty-two paces. Twenty-two both times.
The seal is pretty. The rope is right. I trust what I can check.
Forty, then. I will plan for forty.
Everything is planned twice too long and costs twice too much.
One surveyor who lied
The preacher told me about a surveyor in the north who faked his numbers. A bridge fell. People were hurt.
One surveyor did that. So surveyors cannot be trusted, he says, and I am a surveyor.
Maybe he is right. Maybe you should not trust my numbers either.
One surveyor is not every surveyor. Judge your numbers by checking them.
It is true that one bad surveyor can do great harm, so double-checking everything you measure is only sensible.
That bridge fell because of bad wood, I am sure of it, so the surveyor was probably blamed unfairly.
The preacher tells that story to everyone, and a man who tells scary stories should not be believed.
Judge the numbers, not the trade. Yes.
One man from the north is not me. My head is clearer.
Maybe you should not. I would not.
Sy puts his tripod away.
The children in the rain
The preacher spoke of the children who walk to school in the rain. Their cold little hands. Their wet shoes.
He said a school makes children walk, and walking in rain makes them ill, and could I live with that?
I cried, honestly. I cannot run a school that makes children ill.
Sad pictures are not reasons. Do children who walk to school get ill more?
Wet shoes really are miserable, and if even one child gets ill because of the school, that is one too many.
Children walk in the rain to the bakery too, so the preacher should complain about bread as well.
The preacher has no children of his own, so he has no right to talk about them.
Do they? Forty children walked to my library last winter. None of them caught a cold from walking.
He painted a picture and I stepped into it. Feelings are not reasons.
One too many. Yes. No school.
Ada shuts her book. The children stay untaught, in the dry.
The question he never answered
Ada, the preacher told you the school is a bad idea. Did he say why?
He spoke of the stars, and of humility, and of how small we are.
It was beautiful. I felt very small. Too small to run a school.
But did he answer the question? Why is the school a bad idea?
Humility is a fine thing, and a person who feels small is right to be careful with big plans like a school.
Stars have nothing to do with schools, so the preacher clearly knows nothing about teaching.
If it was beautiful, then he must have been wise, and wise people are worth listening to.
Why is it a bad idea? He never said. He talked about the stars until I forgot the question.
A beautiful speech about the wrong thing is still about the wrong thing.
Careful with big plans. Yes.
Ada looks at the stars. The question stays unanswered.
All the masons agree
The preacher gathered all the masons at the inn. All of them. He asked who thought the next building would stand.
Nobody put a hand up. Not one. When every mason doubts, the doubt must be right.
So I doubt it too.
Nobody raising a hand is not proof. What is wrong with the plan?
When every expert in a room agrees, that is as close to proof as you get, so I would listen to them.
Masons at an inn have been drinking, and drunk men do not count.
They were all afraid of the preacher, so they said nothing, and that means the building is probably fine.
What is wrong with it? I looked at the plan. Nothing. The ground is checked. The stone is good.
A room of quiet men is not a reason. I nearly let it be one.
I doubt it too, then.
Brick puts his trowel down.
The old plan
I spent a month on an old plan before the preacher came. The one with the big tower.
He said the tower would fall. He is right, actually. The base is too narrow.
But a month! I cannot throw away a month. I will build the tower and hope.
The month is spent either way. Is the tower worth building? No.
A month of work is a lot to lose, so the smart thing is to keep the tower and just make the base a little wider.
The preacher only says it will fall because he wants you to fail, so build the tower and prove him wrong.
If it falls, it falls, and at least the month was not wasted.
Is the tower worth building? No. It falls. I knew that.
The month is gone whether I build it or not. That is a hard thing to say out loud.
I will build the tower and hope.
The tower falls in the first storm. The month is still gone.
The preacher's calm spell
The preacher read the sky for me. Three storms hit this valley in three weeks, he said.
So the weather owes us calm. It must be calm for months now. We should start the wheel without the flood wall.
He is good with skies. Let us skip the wall and save the coins.
The sky does not keep score. Three storms do not make calm due.
Three storms in three weeks is very unusual, so it does stand to reason that we are owed a quiet spell.
We should build the flood wall twice as high, because three storms mean this valley is cursed.
The preacher cannot read skies, nobody can, so ignore him and just do whatever is cheapest.
The sky does not keep score. Neither do dice. I said that once, before.
We build the flood wall. Storms do not owe anyone anything.
We skip the wall.
The fourth storm takes the wheel. The sky was not keeping count.
Wood or iron
The preacher says a wheel is either all wood, blessed and old, or all iron, cold and new. There is no other kind.
All iron rusts by the river. So it must be all wood. And all wood is too weak for the big wheel. So no wheel.
Or a wood wheel with iron bands. Two choices were never the only choices.
He knows wheels better than either of us, and if he says there are two kinds, then there are two kinds.
Then iron, and we paint it every month, because a rusty wheel is better than no wheel.
Old blessed wood sounds like nonsense, and a man who blesses wood is not worth listening to.
Wood with iron bands. Of course. Every cart wheel in the valley is made that way.
Two doors, and a window right there. I keep forgetting the window.
No wheel, then.
The miners crush ore by hand for another year.
The builder from nowhere
The preacher asked me where you come from. I did not know. Nobody does.
A builder with no home, he said, has no one to answer to. Such a person will leave the lamp half made and vanish.
I will not start a lamp for someone who might vanish.
Where I come from says nothing about the lamp. Look at what I have built here.
People with no home are often unreliable, that is just true, so it is fair for Iva to want some proof.
The preacher has no home either, he wanders from lodge to lodge, so he should not talk.
I will tell you exactly where I was born, and then you will see that I am trustworthy.
What you have built here. A well. A bridge. A school. A mill.
Where you come from was never the question. What you do is the question.
Some proof. Yes. Bring me proof.
Iva bangs a horseshoe flat. The lamp stays unmade.
Bonfires, as always
The preacher says the cliff bonfires are holy. Every captain for two hundred years lit them.
A lamp of iron and glass would put out a holy flame. Who am I to put out two hundred years of fire?
I forge horseshoes. Horseshoes are old too.
Two hundred years is not a reason. Did the bonfires stop the wrecks?
A thing that people kept doing for two centuries must have worked, or they would have stopped.
The captains lit fires because they had nothing better, and now we do, so they were simply foolish.
Light the lamp only on nights without a bonfire, so the holy fire is never put out.
Did they stop the wrecks? Captain Hale counted twelve last winter.
Old is not the same as right. I forge new things every day.
Who am I. Yes.
Iva goes back to horseshoes. The ships keep hitting the rocks.
A builder like the last one
A preacher told me about a builder who came to a village in the north. He took the jobs, took the coins, and left a half-dug well.
You are a builder too. So you will do the same. No more work for you, I am sorry.
One builder is not every builder. Judge me by the well in the square.
That builder sounds awful, and I understand why you are careful, so I will pay you first and work after.
The preacher made that story up, because preachers say anything to get people scared.
Every village has a story like that, and stories grow in the telling, so it probably never happened at all.
The well in the square. You did dig that, and it is not half.
One builder in the north is not you. The buckets are by the river, if you want the work.
I will pay first... no. No, I will not.
Hana turns back to her oven.
You talk to tricksters
The preacher saw you talking to Pip and to Dodge. Tricksters, both of them.
Anyone who talks with tricksters is a trickster, he says. I do not deal with tricksters. Go away.
Who I talk to says nothing about my work. Look at the fence I fixed.
Pip and Dodge are children, not tricksters, so the preacher is simply wrong about them.
I only talked to them to catch them out, so really I am the opposite of a trickster.
The preacher talks to everyone in the valley, so by his own rule he is a trickster too.
The fence. Straighter than mine, I said so myself.
Who you talk to. Hm. I talk to the goats and I am not a goat. All right.
Go away, I said.
Idris turns his back and counts goats.
Poor Pickle
The preacher says builders frighten goats. Poor Pickle. She would shake all night with your hammering.
I could not bear it. I cannot have you near my cottage any more.
Pickle shaking is a sad picture, not a reason. Has she shaken once since the well?
You are right, I would never want to frighten her, so I will keep away from the cottage.
Goats do not have feelings like that, so there is nothing to worry about.
The preacher does not even like goats, so why would he care about Pickle?
Since the well? She slept through the whole thing. Right by the site.
He made me picture her shaking. Nothing shook. Come by when you like, dear.
Keep away, then. Thank you.
Sal shuts the cottage door.
The bruised apples
The day after you crossed the new bridge, half my apples came up bruised.
The preacher says the bridge shakes the ground and bruises the fruit. It came first. So it did it. No more work for you.
The bridge came first. Did it bruise the apples? What else changed?
Bridges do carry heavy carts and heavy carts do shake the ground, so the preacher may well be right.
Apples bruise when you pick them badly, so this is your fault and not the bridge.
The preacher wants the bridge gone because he hates anything new, so ignore him.
What else changed? There was hail that night. Small hail. I forgot the hail.
Hail bruises apples. Bridges do not. Coming first is not causing.
He may well be right. Go.
Pia sorts bruised apples and blames the bridge.
With the preacher or against him
The preacher says you are either with the valley or with the builders. I am with the valley.
So I cannot be with you. That is how it is, one or the other.
Why only two? Builders can be with the valley. The bridge is for the valley.
If I have to pick, then I pick the valley too, and you can keep your scarecrow money.
The preacher is not from the valley, so he does not get to say who is with it.
I am with the valley more than you are, because I built the well and you only grow beans.
The bridge is for the valley. My carts cross it.
One or the other. Or both. He never said both.
You can keep it. Yes.
Ren goes back to arguing with Rin.
The whole lane agrees
Everyone on our lane says the preacher is right about you. Every single house.
When the whole lane agrees, that is that. I cannot take your milk any more.
A whole lane agreeing is not proof. What did the preacher say I did?
If every house on the lane agrees, then I must have done something, and I am sorry for it.
The lane has four houses, and four people are hardly everyone.
They only agree because they are afraid of him, so their opinion is worthless.
What did he say you did? He did not say. He said everyone knew.
Everyone knew, and nobody knew what. I will take the milk.
Something. Yes. Go away, please.
Rin looks at the neighbours and says nothing.
One builder, then a city
The preacher sat in my inn all evening. One builder, he said, brings a school. A school brings students. Students bring noise, noise brings a city, and a city eats an inn like mine.
So I cannot help a builder. It ends with my inn gone.
Each step needs its own proof. Does a school really bring a city?
It is true that towns do grow, and a careful innkeeper should think about where it all ends.
A city would bring more guests, so you should want a city and thank the builder.
The preacher drank three bowls of your soup and did not pay, so why do you listen to him?
Does a school bring a city? Market Town is still Market Town.
He ran the steps together. I ran with him. Sit down, have some soup.
Where it all ends. Yes. Go on now.
Dot wipes the same table twice.
The seal on the letter
The preacher brought a letter with a seal. It says builders need a permit from the Grey Order.
A seal is a seal. I cannot stamp anything for you until you have their permit.
A seal is not a law. Which law says builders need their permit?
Seals are serious things, and a clerk who ignores one could lose his job, so I understand you.
Anyone can melt wax and press a ring in it, so the letter is obviously fake.
I will go and get their permit, then, if that is what the letter says.
Which law? I have every law in this hall. None of them says it.
A seal is wax. A law is a law. I had them muddled.
I understand too, but I still cannot stamp it.
Ossian files the letter under "important".
The preacher's pamphlets
I paid the preacher forty coins for a box of pamphlets about the dangers of builders.
Forty coins! If I sell to a builder now, the forty coins were for nothing. So no rope, no nails, no oil for you.
The forty coins are gone either way. Does refusing me earn them back?
Forty coins is a lot for a small shop, so it makes sense to get your money's worth out of the pamphlets.
The preacher cheated you, and a cheated person should never trust anyone again.
Sell the pamphlets to me, then, and you will have your forty back.
Does it earn them back? No. It just loses me a customer too.
Gone is gone. I will use the pamphlets to wrap nails.
My money's worth. Yes. No sale.
Nell straightens a pile of pamphlets nobody buys.
You want to close the mine
The preacher says a mill means you want to close the mine and put every miner out of work.
You said you wanted to crush ore faster. Faster means fewer miners. Fewer means none. I heard it from him. No oil for you.
That is not what I said. A mill crushes ore. It does not dig it.
I would never close the mine, I promise, and I will hire every miner myself if I have to.
Fewer miners might be a good thing, honestly, because the mine is dangerous.
The preacher has never been down a mine, so he knows nothing about it.
It does not dig it. The miners dig. The mill only crushes.
He put words in your mouth, and I heard them in his voice. Take the oil.
No oil. I said.
Tam turns back to the shift board.
Due for a cave-in
The preacher counted for me. Twelve safe months in this mine. Twelve! A cave-in is due, he says, and builders bring bad luck.
I cannot let a builder near the cart while a cave-in is due.
Twelve safe months do not make a cave-in due. Rock does not keep count.
Twelve months is a long run of luck, so being extra careful right now is only sensible.
Cave-ins come from bad timber, and the timber is fine, so there will never be one.
The preacher is not a miner, so he cannot say anything about cave-ins.
Rock does not keep count. It does not know about months.
I put a calendar on a mountain. Silly. The cart needs its wheel.
Extra careful. Yes. Stay away.
Quill checks the roof again, for the tenth time today.
What about the stew?
Mab, why will you not take the ore basket from me any more?
Have you tasted the stew today? The preacher says the carrots are too small. Look at the carrots!
Tiny. And the onions. Do not get me started on the onions.
The carrots can wait. Why will you not take the ore?
Those are small carrots, you are right, and I think the onions look a bit sad too.
The preacher knows nothing about cooking, so his carrot opinion is worthless.
If the stew is bad, then the miners will be grumpy, and grumpy miners are the real problem here.
Why? He said builders are trouble. He did not say why. Then we talked about carrots.
I never asked him why. I will take the ore.
The onions. Yes. Exactly.
You talk about onions for a long time. The ore basket stays full.
My father's harbour
The preacher says builders will change the harbour, and my father's harbour will be gone forever. He said it very softly.
I cried. I cannot help anyone who would erase my father.
Missing your father is real, but not a reason. Would a lighthouse erase him?
I would never want to hurt your father's memory, so I will leave the harbour as it is.
Your father is gone and the harbour is not his any more, so let it go.
The preacher used your father to make you cry, and a man who does that is wicked.
Would it erase him? He rowed out in the dark every winter. A light would have brought him home.
The preacher made me cry and called it a reason. The oar job is yours.
Leave it as it is. Yes.
Orla looks at the sea.
Fish are sold by hand
The preacher says fish were always sold by the fisher, on the quay, by hand. Always.
Carrying crates for the Tavern is not the old way. So no crates for you.
Always is not a reason. Does the crate get the fish there fresh?
The old ways do keep a harbour together, and I would not want to be the one who broke them.
Everyone else sends crates to the Tavern, so you are the odd one out.
The preacher has never sold a fish, so he cannot know how fish are sold.
Fresh? Fresher than waiting on the quay all day, yes.
Always is a long time to do the wrong thing. Take the crate.
I would not break them either. Go.
Lin sells fish by hand, slowly.
The preacher's cookbook
The preacher has a cookbook older than the Tavern. It says a cook must never take goods from strangers.
A book that old must be right. So no ledger, no fish, nothing from you.
An old book is not a reason. Does it say why?
Old cookbooks hold a lot of wisdom, and a cook would be foolish to ignore one.
You should burn that book, because old books are always full of nonsense.
I am not a stranger, we met last week, so the book does not apply to me.
Does it say why? It says "it is written". That is all it says.
A book that old, and that is the reason. I will take the ledger.
Foolish to ignore. Yes.
Bea stirs the chowder and does not look up.
